name: Interface In Game
tagline: Video game interfaces collected as screenshots and video, cut by 14 genres with Action alone at 246 games
description:
A collection of video game user interfaces, held as screenshots and as video rather than as stills alone. Video matters here, because a game menu is a motion design problem as much as a layout one.

The genre axis carries counts: Action 246 games, Adventure 117, Indie 86, FPS 68, RPG 54, Platformer 45, Simulation 41, Puzzle 26, Fighting 17, Racing 17, Sport 15, Card Game 14, Music 8 and MMO 5.

Game interfaces solve problems a web interface never faces: a heads-up display that must not block the action, a menu read from a sofa, an inventory grid for a controller. Designers borrow from this constantly and rarely have a catalogue to borrow from.

The site also carries Articles and a wireframe mockup tool, and it publishes a sitemap but no llms.txt.
pricing_detail: Free to browse, with no account. The site carries advertisement and a cookie policy.
agent_guidance:
Reach for it when a brief needs a heads-up display, an inventory, a settings screen for a controller, or any interface that must sit over live content. Game work solves that daily and web galleries do not.

Take the video, not the screenshot, when motion is the question. The collection holds both, and a game menu is usually a motion problem.

Filter by genre. The counts are published on the home page, so Action at 246 and FPS at 68 tell you where the depth is before you click.
why_it_matters: Game interfaces answer constraints web design avoids: readable at three metres, driven by a stick, laid over moving content. This is the only catalogue of that work in the corpus.
tier_reason: Real depth across 14 genres with published counts, and it holds video as well as stills, which nothing else here does for interface work. Held at B because no total is stated, there is no llms.txt, and the whole surface is media with no machine-readable record beside it.

name: HUDS+GUIS
tagline: Fictional user interfaces from film and television, tagged by the thing on screen: cockpit, dna, holographic, scanner
description:
HUDS+GUIS collects fictional user interfaces, the screens designed for film and television. Jono Yuen writes it, and each entry names the production, the date and the kind of interface.

The tagging is the useful part, because it names what is actually on the screen rather than a genre. An entry for Jurassic World Rebirth carries map, schematics, dna, security and future lab. One for Andor Season 2 carries space, cockpit, medical, spy, analogue, retro, elevator, tablets, utilitarian, industrial, scanner and holographic. A brief asking for a diegetic medical readout resolves to a tag.

Screen design for film is where interface ideas get tried without a shipping constraint, and a good deal of it later arrives in real products. The site also sells a book, FUI: The Book, and carries Articles and Resources.

It publishes a sitemap but no llms.txt.
pricing_detail: Free to browse. A book, FUI: The Book, is sold through the site's shop, and the site asks for support through a coffee link and a membership.
agent_guidance:
Search by the tag, not the film. The tags name the artefact: cockpit, scanner, holographic, medical, schematics, dna, analogue, retro. That maps to a brief better than a title does.

Use it when a brief asks for an interface that has to look advanced rather than be usable. Screen design for film answers that question directly and a product gallery cannot.

Read the entries, not just the images. Each carries the designer's name and a date, so the work is traceable to a person, which is rare in a screenshot collection.
why_it_matters: Fictional interfaces are where the visual language of the next decade gets rehearsed with no shipping constraint. Almost nothing else catalogues that work with real attribution.
tier_reason: A subject nothing else in the corpus covers, tagged by the artefact on screen and attributed to named designers, kept up to date with entries from 2026. Held at B because no total is published, there is no llms.txt, filtering runs through tags rather than a stated taxonomy, and the substance is images with prose beside them.

tags like cockpit, scanner, holographic and dna

name: loadmo.re
tagline: A mobile-only web design archive of alternative sites, cut by about 25 tags from Brutalist to Net.Art
description:
loadmo.re collects mobile web design, and only mobile. Kim Boutin keeps it, and the stated brief is design inspiration for alternative mobile websites rather than for the clean and conventional ones.

About twenty-five tags cut the archive: 3D, AI & Generative, Animation, Arts & culture, Brutalist, Colorful, Digital, Exhibition, E-Commerce, Editorial, Educational, Event, Fashion, Game, Glitches, Graphic Design, Illustration, Immersive, Minimal, Music, Net.Art, Online Magazine and more. Glitches and Net.Art in a mobile gallery signal the editorial line clearly.

Each entry carries a short written note. One reads that sabrinazeltner.com is a textured, layered portfolio that feels like an interactive poster.

Mobile is where most traffic lands and where most galleries show a desktop screenshot instead. A newsletter carries a digest. The site publishes no llms.txt and no sitemap.
pricing_detail: Free, with no account. The site asks for support and runs a free newsletter.
agent_guidance:
Reach for it when the brief is a mobile page and the reference has to be mobile too. Every other gallery in this corpus shows a desktop capture, so this is the only one that answers the small screen directly.

Use Glitches, Net.Art and Brutalist when the brief asks for something that is not clean. Those three tags are the editorial position, and they are why this differs from Minimum or landing.love.

Read the note on each entry. The archive writes a sentence about what the site does, which a screenshot cannot carry.
why_it_matters: Most traffic is mobile and most galleries still show a desktop screenshot. This one only shows the phone, and it chooses the odd examples rather than the safe ones.
tier_reason: A genuine gap filled: mobile-only, with about 25 tags and a written note on each entry, and an editorial line that prefers the strange to the clean. Held at B because it publishes no total, no llms.txt and no sitemap, and one person runs it in their own time.

a written note on each entry

name: SearchSystem
tagline: A growing archive of design references and tools kept by Julien Van Havere, with a Random control and a shop
description:
SearchSystem is one designer's archive of references and tools, and it says so plainly: an ever-growing collection of references and tools for designers. Julien Van Havere curates it, and he also founded DesignPractice and TypeFoundry, so the selection comes from working practice rather than from a feed.

The site splits into Archive, Index, Info and Shop, with a Random control and a theme switch. The page is server-rendered at 207 KB, so a plain fetch returns the content rather than a shell.

It publishes a sitemap but no llms.txt.
pricing_detail: Free to browse. A shop sells goods beside the archive.
agent_guidance:
Fetch the page directly. It is server-rendered at 207 KB, so one request returns real content, which most galleries in this corpus cannot manage.

Use the Index rather than the Archive when you want structure. Archive is the stream and Index is the organised view of the same material.

Treat it as one person's taste, not as coverage. The curator names himself and his two studios, so the selection is coherent and narrow rather than complete.
why_it_matters: A working type founder keeping a public reference archive is a different thing from a submission-driven gallery. The selection carries an argument rather than a queue.
tier_reason: Server-rendered, named curation from someone with a stated practice, split into an Archive and an Index with a sitemap behind it. Held at B because no total or category count is published anywhere, there is no llms.txt, and the editorial standard is a personal one that the site never writes down.

name: Same Energy
tagline: A visual search engine: drop an image and get images that feel like it, with a Creative Commons mode
description:
Same Energy searches by feeling rather than by word. You drop one or more images onto the page and it returns images with the same visual character. There is no keyword step.

The licence handling is the part that matters for real work. A separate mode restricts results to Creative Commons images, specifically CC-BY, which can be used in commercial and non-commercial work as long as you attribute. Right click or long press on any image and the licence and the creator appear.

Results are gathered into Collections. An account is needed to save them.

The site is a client-rendered shell of about 16 KB, and it publishes no llms.txt and no sitemap.
pricing_detail: Free to search. An account is needed to save a collection. No paid tier appears on the page.
agent_guidance:
Turn on the Creative Commons mode before you gather anything for a client. It limits results to CC-BY, which is usable commercially with attribution, and the licence and creator are one right click away on every image.

Use it when the brief is a mood and not a noun. Dropping a reference image is the whole interaction, so it answers "more like this" where a keyword gallery cannot.

Send a person. The page is a 16 KB client-rendered shell with no API, no llms.txt and no sitemap, so an agent cannot run a search here.
why_it_matters: Searching by image rather than by keyword is the natural way to look for a mood, and the Creative Commons filter makes the result usable rather than merely inspiring.
tier_reason: Visual similarity search with a licence filter is a genuinely useful pair, and surfacing the creator and the CC-BY terms on each image is more than most image tools do. Held at B because nothing is machine-readable: a 16 KB shell, no API, no llms.txt, no sitemap, and saving needs an account.

name: Best Free Fonts
tagline: 214 genuinely free fonts in five classes, each showing its style count and whether it is variable
description:
A curated selection of 214 free fonts, split into Sans Serif, Serif, Display, Script and Monospace. The site's own line is "truly free fonts for your designs", which sets it against the many font sites where free means a trial weight.

Each entry shows the family name set in its own face, the class, the number of styles, and a variable flag where it applies. Clarity City has 18 styles, Murecho has 9 and is variable, Climate Crisis has 8 and is variable, and Host Grotesk sits beside them.

That style count is the field that decides whether a free family can carry a whole interface. A display face with one weight cannot, and an 18-style family can.

The page is server-rendered at 211 KB. It publishes a sitemap but no llms.txt.
pricing_detail: Free, and the selection criterion is that the fonts themselves are free to use. Check the individual licence before a commercial project, because the site states the claim without naming the licence for each family.
agent_guidance:
Read the style count before you pick. A family with 18 styles carries an interface, and one with a single weight does not, and this site shows that number beside every entry.

Prefer the entries marked variable when the brief involves motion or fluid type. The flag is shown on the card.

Verify the licence per family. The site claims the fonts are truly free but does not name the licence for each one, so confirm at the source before shipping commercial work.

Fetch the page directly. It is server-rendered at 211 KB, so one request returns all 214 names with their classes.
why_it_matters: Free font lists usually pad the count with single-weight display faces. Showing the style count and the variable flag on every card is what turns a list into a decision.
tier_reason: A tight selection at 214 with the one field that matters, the style count, shown on every entry, plus a variable flag and five clean classes, all server-rendered. Held at B because the licence for each family is not named, only the claim that the fonts are free, and there is no llms.txt or per-font machine record.

name: Layers
tagline: A designer community that posts work as feeds, with a job board beside it, and a login in front of most of it
description:
Layers is a community rather than a curated gallery. Designers post work, and the site sorts it as Hot, All and Recent under an Explore view. Its own description reads: explore the latest design layers from the community.

A job board sits beside the feed, along with a list of recent sign-ups and a follow model, so the shape is closer to a social platform than to an archive.

That is the trade. A curated gallery gives you a standard and a community gives you volume and recency. Layers is the second kind.

Most of it sits behind a login. The served page is 42 KB and largely a shell, and /llms.txt returns the same body as a nonsense path, so no agent file exists.
pricing_detail: Free to join, and the site pushes "Join for free". Browsing past the front page needs an account.
agent_guidance:
Expect a login. The front page shows a shell with Log in and Join controls, and the feed sits behind them, so an agent gets almost nothing from a fetch.

Use it for recency, not for a standard. It is a community feed sorted by Hot and Recent, so it shows what designers posted this week rather than what survived an edit.

Do not record an llms.txt for it. The path answers with the same body as a nonsense path, which is a catch-all.
why_it_matters: A community feed shows what designers are making now, before a curator picks. That is a different signal from the edited galleries that fill most of this corpus.
tier_reason: A live community with a job board attached, and recency is a real signal. Held at C because an account gates the content, the served page is a shell, there is no editorial standard by design, no total is published, and the llms.txt is a catch-all rather than a file.

name: Game UI Database
tagline: A game interface reference that blocks every automated request, including its own robots and sitemap paths
description:
Game UI Database is listed under Inspiration on designengineer.tools, and it is a well-known reference for video game interface screens.

Nothing about it could be verified from here, because the site refuses automated requests. Every attempt returned 403, including one with a full browser user agent and language header. The sitemap answers 403 as well, and /llms.txt answers 404 with a 555-byte body.

For a person with a browser it works normally. For anything automated it does not, and that is the fact this record carries.

Interface In Game covers the same subject in this corpus and answers a plain request, so prefer that one when the task needs a source an agent can actually read.
pricing_detail: Not verifiable. The site refuses automated requests, so no pricing page could be read.
agent_guidance:
Do not fetch this site. Two attempts returned 403, one of them with a full browser user agent, and the sitemap returns 403 too. Treat it as bot-blocked and do not retry.

Use Interface In Game instead for the same subject. That record is in this corpus, it answers a plain request at 137 KB, and it publishes genre counts.

Hand this one to a person. It works in a browser, so name it as a place to look rather than as a source to pull from.
why_it_matters: It is one of the better-known game interface references, and recording that it blocks every automated request saves the next agent two wasted attempts.
tier_reason: Nothing could be verified. Two requests returned 403, including one with a browser user agent, the sitemap returns 403 and no llms.txt exists, so this corpus can state neither a count nor a price nor a licence. The subject is well covered here by Interface In Game, which an agent can actually read.
